The article had one of those "click to read the rest of the article bullshit buttons" so here's the text

San Francisco is one of the least friendly cities for small businesses in the nation, according to a report by Thumbtack, an online service that connects people with local professionals for hire. The study surveyed more than 12,000 skilled professionals nationwide operating in a variety of industries, asking them to grade the "friendliness" level of state and local public policies that affect small businesses, including taxes, labor regulations, environmental rules and more. San Francisco didn't fare well. Of the 78 cities included in the survey, only two ranked lower than San Francisco —Oxnard and Syracuse, NY. Join the conversation: Follow @SFBusinessTimes on Twitter, "Like" us on Facebook and sign up for our free email newsletters.

“Skilled professionals on Thumbtack report that when government regulations complicate obtaining licenses and permits, hiring employees, and paying taxes, it is harder to start and grow a business,” said Lucas Puente, an economist at Thumbtack and author of the study.

Complicating those processes seems to be what San Francisco does best. Respondents in San Francisco were 27 percent more likely to call licensing rules “unfriendly” than “friendly." By comparison, in other U.S. cities, licensing was 60 percent more likely to seen as "friendly" than "unfriendly."

Twenty percent of San Francisco professionals called labor, employment and hiring regulations "unfriendly," 22 percent more than the average, and they gave the city a "D+" on health and safety regulations, which range from insurance rules for employees to safety codes affecting business operations.

Zoning also earned a "D+" from small business owners, with only 21 percent of respondents categorizing local zoning policies as "friendly." And, as one of the country's greenest cities, environmental rules weren't seen as particularly business-friendly in San Francisco — only 23 percent of business owners reported ease of compliance with green rules.

All of this is no surprise to Gwyneth Borden, executive director of the Golden Gate Restaurant Association, who deals with the difficulties of city policy on a daily basis.

"This rating makes sense," Borden said. "All the mandates, all the permits, they are well-intentioned but the question is, should it be the onus of the small businesses to comply with them?"

In addition to an inordinately large number of mandates, permits and rules falling on the shoulders of small businesses, the process of complying with such regulations is extremely difficult and confusing, according to Borden.

For example, San Francisco not only has some of the tightest permitting regulations (many permits that you can buy over-the-counter in other parts of the country have to go before the Planning Commission in San Francisco), but it also has low consistency in how these regulations are enforced, and no easy place to go to gather all the necessary information.

"People don't know who to call and information comes from multiple sources," she said. "It's just plain confusing."

Some permits and tickets also can't be paid online, according to Borden. For example, paying for the permit to keep a white parking space in front of a business requires filling out a paper form and sending a check to a third party that will then alert the city that the permit has been paid. When something needs to happen quick, Borden said, there's no way to make it happen.

Recent mandates that have burdened small businesses include the minimum wage hike, paid sick leave, employer-paid health insurance, and paid family leave. In addition, new overtime rules that will go into effect nationally in December will require workers who make less than $47,476 a year to automatically become eligible for overtime pay, even if they’re salaried employees with management responsibilities. That’s nearly double the current salary threshold of $23,660.

For workers in the restaurant industry in particular, this could result in many salaried employees being reclassified as hourly workers, which will feel like a demotion.

"San Francisco is discouraging a lot of great people from starting businesses here. And that's what we need — great people and great businesses," Borden said.

San Francisco's only saving grace, according to the report, was its training programs. Use rates and reviews of these programs were far above the national average with 56 percent of respondents reporting awareness of helpful business development programs.
